This paper is concerned with the three-parameter Weibull distribution which is widely
used as a model in reliability and lifetime studies. In practice, the Weibull model parame-
ters are not known in advance and must be estimated from a random sample. Difficulties in
applying the method of maximum likelihood to three-parameter Weibull models have led
to a variety of alternative approaches in the literature. In this paper we consider the non-
linear weighted errors-in-variables (EIV) fitting approach. As a main result, two theorems
on the existence of the EIV estimate are obtained. An illustrative example is also included.
The Weibull distribution is one of the most widely used model in reliability and lifetime studies (see [8,16–18]). This dis-
tribution was introduced by the Swedish statistician Waloddi Weibull who used it for the first time in 1939 in connection
with his studies on the strength of materials (see [24]). Two popular forms of this skewed distribution are two- and three-

Statistical estimation of unknown parameters from a random sample is an important problem that can be solved by many
methods. Maximum likelihood (ML) estimation is a traditional method for parameter estimation since it possesses beneficial
properties such as asymptotic normality and consistency. But, the ML estimate does not necessarily exist, and it is not nec-
essarily unique. For the two-parameter Weibull distribution, the results of Pratt [19] and Burridge [5] guarantee the exis-
tence of a unique ML estimate. However, our attention here is focused on the three-parameter Weibull distribution. In
this case many additional difficulties arise. For example, there is no standard ML estimate for any observation from density
(2) (see e.g. [12,16]). In the literature, considerable effort has been devoted to such difficulties with the maximum likelihood
approach (see e.g. [1,2,7,23]). There are several other statistical methods for estimating model parameters such as the meth-
od of moments, the method of percentiles and the Bayesian method. Unfortunately, none of these methods (excluding the
Bayesian one) is appropriate for small data sets (see [16–18]).
A very popular method for parameter estimation is the least squares (LS) method. The problem of nonlinear weighted
least squares fitting of the three-parameter Weibull distribution to the given data

exactly. In such situation, when also the observations of the independent variable contain errors,
then it seems reasonable to estimate the unknown parameters so that the weighted sum of squares of all errors is minimized.
This approach, known as errors-in-variables regression (EIV regression), is a natural generalization of the LS regression (see
e.g. [9]). In numerical analysis, errors-in-variables regression is known as the total least squares method (see [10]).
Numerical methods for solving the nonlinear EIV problem are described in Boggs et al. [6] and Schwetlick and Tiller [21].
Before the iterative minimization of the sum of squares it is still necessary to ask whether the EIV estimate exists. In the case
of nonlinear EIV problems it is still extremely difficult to answer this question (see [4,13,14]).
The authors have so far not come across any paper dealing with a nonlinear EIV fitting problem for the three-parametric
Weibull distribution, in spite of the many papers on Weibull models. The structure of the paper is as follows. In Section 2, we
